zones.label: Column 1, part 1
zones.note: Lexical cross-check after independent scan reading: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, supplied page subset, CC BY 4.0. Dataset: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . Used as a vocabulary aid, not as a replacement transcription; this copy’s spelling and typography remain scan-grounded.

lines.note: Irui is explained by cotonaru taguy, a different kind or class, rather than the clothing sense at the foot of f271. The Portuguese begins “another kind, or species,” with eſpe- continued below.
The first syllable completes eſpecie. Irui, iguiǒ then introduces diverse kinds or forms, illustrated here by different species of animals; the caron on ǒ is visible.

The animal-species gloss ends here. Permet. introduces a transferred application to diverse appearances or dress. The example is visibly deta- / chi, not silently expanded to the more familiar idetachi.
Chi completes detachi across the physical break. The Portuguese explains the example as attire and clothing of various kinds, connecting the “different forms” expression to dress.

runs.text: P. Palaura que ſe vſa nas Vtas por

lines.note: The enlarged I was omitted by the bootstrap; it belongs to the headword ISa and extends beside the following row. P. marks poetic usage. Vtas, Japanese uta poems, occurs inside the Portuguese explanation, which describes a word used for stylistic grace rather than assigning an ordinary prose gloss.
This completes the explanation of ISa as an expression used in poetry for grace or elegance. The continuation is inset beside the enlarged initial, not a separate dictionary entry.
Iſacai gives the verb “to dispute or contend,” with its inflected forms. Both rounded-vowel marks are carons, and the headword's long ſ is distinct from f.
This separate nominal entry means a dispute or contention, corresponding to the preceding verb. The narrow first letter is capital I, not lowercase i.
Iſago means sand; the gloss specifies the sand of the beach. Historical Portuguese Area is retained rather than modernized to areia, and the headword begins with capital I.
Iſaguiyoi is glossed as clean and pure. The transferred application continues in the next row. The right margin shows per without a terminal hyphen, so the OCR's hyphen is not retained.
Met. completes the divided permet. label. Cocorono iſaguiyoi fito describes a person pure of heart; Homẽ is the printed nasal-abbreviated Portuguese form beginning its explanation.
The Portuguese completes “a person of a pure and clean heart,” making the moral application of the preceding adjective explicit. The nasal sign in coração remains over the printed vowel.
This indented derivative supplies the adverbial form associated with Iſaguiyoi. It has no separate Portuguese gloss; the circumflex in yô is retained as printed.
The following indented form is the corresponding noun in -ſa, purity or cleanness in the senses just given. The long ſ must not be confused with f.
Iſai denotes detail or minuteness and, adverbially, doing something in detail. The scan supports meudamente, correcting OCR meudameme; the example begins with a second Iſai at the right edge.
With the preceding Iſai, cocoroyeta means “I have understood in detail.” The Portuguese repeats that meaning and abbreviates the nasal in the ending of meudamẽte.
Iſamaxiguſa is a poetic name for the pine, equated with Matçu. The initial capital and the guſa sequence are visible; this is not an inflection of the next adjective Iſamaxij.
Iſamaxij is described as cheerful, lively, or alert. These glosses set up the following exhortation to serve one's lord energetically; modern “brave” is not substituted for the dictionary's wording.
The paragraph example begins Iſamaxij, not OCR Mamaxij. It calls for an eager or spirited heart in service; gofôcôuo is the honorific expression for service, with both printed circumflexes preserved.
Mǒxe completes the exhortation: serve the lord with cheerfulness and effort. The Portuguese is printed with Seruiao joined, and its abbreviated cõ is retained rather than expanded.
This indented derivative is the noun in -ſa, the quality of being spirited or lively. The source clearly begins Iſ-, correcting the bootstrap Mſ-.
The associated adverbial form stands on its own indented row. Its accent is a descending grave, ù, which is retained rather than regularized from Japanese morphology.
Iſame means to admonish, rebuke, or exhort, with the following forms illustrating its conjugation. The example introduced by Vt continues over three physical rows.
Canefuſa, a personal name, is admonished by these words. Iſamerare is the passive form of the lemma; youai begins the phrase “weak heart” continued in the next row.

Cocorouo fiqitatete describes raising or rallying that weak heart. The printed italic Cum. is retained before the Portuguese explanation, without expanding it or identifying a source not established by the scan; ſen- continues as ſendo below.

runs.text: do reprendido com eſtas palauras, tomou animo.

lines.note: This completes ſendo and states that, admonished by these words, the man took courage. It confirms that the Japanese example concerns encouragement through reproof, not merely accusation.
The nominal Iſame denotes a rebuke or exhortation. Both Portuguese nouns retain their printed nasal signs over the final o, and l, offers the alternative gloss.
This verb means to become excited or roused, or to spur oneself on. The capital I and caron in ǒda are visible; the next two rows give a military illustration.

The Japanese describes warriors who are fiercely stirred to action. Tçuuamono domo is plural “warriors”; the Portuguese begins the divided word for soldiers, continued in the following row. The small terminal mark after Sol is retained as in the supplied reading.

runs.text: dados que ſe eſpertaõ & aluoroçaõ ferozmente.

lines.note: Dados completes Soldados across the preceding punctuation-marked break. The gloss describes soldiers rousing themselves fiercely. A visible nasal sign over the final o of eſpertaõ, absent from the bootstrap, is restored.
This nominal Iſami means joy or high spirits. The example begins iſamini iſǒ / de, using the preceding verb's form across the row boundary; no unprinted hyphen is added after iſǒ.
De completes iſǒde; vori tatta describes leaping down or out. The Portuguese explicitly says that the person jumped out of the vessel with great spirit, retaining the printed joined cõgrãde.
The explanation ends with excitement and courage, qualifying the leap from the boat in the preceding row. The cedilla in aluoroço is visible and is restored from OCR aluoroco.
Iſami yorocobi combines being roused with rejoicing. The inflected form is printed ôda with a circumflex, unlike the caron-marked form in the preceding Iſami entry; the distinction is preserved.
This completes the gloss “to become excited and rejoice greatly.” It belongs to the compound Iſami yorocobi, not the following fishing term.

runs.text: O peſcar de noite com fogo. Vt,

lines.note: Iſari is fishing at night using a fire. The example starts Iſa- and continues the headword with the object particle and ſuru in the next row; the printed hyphen is retained.
Together with Iſa- above, riuo ſuru means to engage in this form of night fishing. This short roman continuation is an example, not another lemma or a Portuguese phrase.

runs.text: Fogo que fazem denoite os peſcadores

lines.note: Iſaribi denotes the fire made by fishers at night. The compound's -bi element corresponds to fire, while denoite is visibly joined in the Portuguese and is not respaced.
The purpose phrase completes the description of the fishing fire: it is made in order to fish. Historical pera is retained rather than modern para.
Iſaſaca means a very little amount. The second occurrence has a long ſ rather than OCR capital I; na- starts the following naritomo construction, meaning “even though it is only a little.”

runs.text: Ainda que ſeja couſa pouca, ou leue.

lines.note: Ritomo completes naritomo across the break. The Portuguese explains the concessive sense: even though the thing is small in amount or slight in importance.
Iſaſacamo extends the preceding small-amount expression. The scan supplies the omitted capital I, and the Portuguese begins a usage restriction completed below.
The dictionary says that Iſaſacamo is commonly used with negatives. Its example, zonjenu, means not to know, yielding “I do not know the slightest thing.”

runs.text: Nenhũa couſa ſei, ou nemhum tamanino ſei

lines.note: The Portuguese paraphrases the example as knowing nothing, or not even the tiniest amount. The printed forms Nenhũa, nemhum and tamanino are retained, with no terminal punctuation supplied at the right edge.

Iſaſacamotte is another form with the same preceding sense. The scan supplies the missing a between the two long-ſ syllables, and the second pass confirms two t types in motte. Both omissions in the bootstrap iſſacamote are corrected without modernizing the spelling.

Iſaſame is equated with Cariſome, something slight, casual or temporary. P. is visibly upright here within the roman introductory material, unlike the italic opening label in column 1; the capital I is restored.
The second Portuguese gloss is “on loan” or “borrowed,” illustrating the temporary character of Cariſome. It continues the preceding entry rather than beginning a new one.

runs.text: Hum peixe do mar aßi chamado.

lines.note: Iſaza names a sea fish according to this dictionary. The generic historical gloss is retained without assigning a modern species, and aßi preserves the printed double-s ligature.
Iſo means the shore or beach. The example describes going out to enjoy oneself there, and the Portuguese infinitive Ir begins its translation at the right edge.

The first phrase completes “go to amuse oneself at the shore.” Iſoſuru then means gathering shellfish; both apparent f forms in the bootstrap are the long ſ of iſo and ſuru, as the scan and the shore vocabulary confirm.

The Portuguese says that in the Cami region the expression is Iſouo xexeru. Cami and the cited Japanese expression are embedded in that explanation. The final Itẽ is followed by a visible comma, not the bootstrap period.
The same expression, cited as the subject of the Portuguese sentence, also has a transferred use. The following row explains to whom it is applied; Iſouo begins with a long ſ rather than f.

runs.text: ocupão em couſas de pouca importancia.

lines.note: The transferred sense applies to people occupied with matters of little importance. This completes the regional-expression entry and is not part of the next headword about differing appearance.
Iſǒ is paraphrased as cotonaru catachi, a different form or appearance, and glossed as difference in dress. The first letter is capital I and the following letter long ſ, correcting bootstrap ifǒ.

The comparison continues with custom and other respects in which someone differs from others. The historical singular custume and unexpanded &c are preserved, as is the preceding row's printed period after trajo.
Iſô here means a foreign monk, explained by Icocuno bǒzu. The headword begins Iſ-, not Aſ-, and its circumflex distinguishes this printing from the caron-marked appearance word above.
The gloss completes “a foreign religious, or one from another kingdom.” It confirms that bǒzu concerns a monk rather than merely a traveler from elsewhere.
Iſobata denotes the edge of the shore. Although the o is lightly printed, the surviving round shape and the following beach-edge synonym support the supplied headword.
Iſobe is given the same shore-edge meaning as Iſobata. The short Idem gloss refers directly to the previous entry, not to the foreign monk farther above.
Iſocu is equated with Xichiguachi, the seventh lunar month. The scan has the t of Septima, lost in OCR Sepima; lũa retains its nasal abbreviation.
Iſogauaxij describes something hurried or pressed for time. Its following two indented derivatives belong to this adjective; apreßada retains the historical ligature.
This indented -ſa noun denotes the state of being hurried or busy. The ending is a long ſ plus a, not the bootstrap -ta; the first part of gaua is lightly printed but recoverable.

The corresponding adverbial form is supplied without another gloss. Enlargement shows a strong left stroke and a much weaker right trace in the vowel mark, compatible with the supplied caron ǔ, which is retained.
Iſogaxij receives the same meaning as Iſogauaxij: hurried or busy. This shorter adjective begins a new lemma with its own nominal and adverbial derivatives below.
The noun in -ſa corresponds to Iſogaxij. The tall curved letter is long ſ rather than f, correcting the bootstrap Iſogaxifa.
This is the accompanying adverbial form. Its caron is distinctly visible above the final vowel; it remains a separate indented physical row.
Iſogui is the verb “to hurry.” The example begins Vmani, “to/on the horse”; the whole Japanese word is upright in the scan, correcting the bootstrap's alternating italic fragments.

runs.text: muchi vtte momini môde iſoida. D

lines.note: The example describes striking the horse with a whip and pressing it onward, with iſoida as the past form of the lemma; the apparent f is long ſ. Dan begins Portuguese Dando below, without a visible hyphen. Its upright D and densely inked final n retain the supplied mixed-type reading; the final letter's font is less secure than the text.

runs.text: do com a vara no caualo, & apertando lhe as

lines.note: Do completes Dando and explains giving the horse the whip while squeezing it with the legs. The printed apertando lhe remains separated rather than acquiring modern hyphenation.

The sentence finishes with the legs and the resulting haste. The scan's paired long-ſ forms in preſſouſe replace OCR fſ, while its unusual separation a preſſouſe is preserved rather than normalized to a modern spelling.
Isǒjin and isǒmono name a person who is unusual or eccentric. Unlike the nearby Iſǒ lemma, both s letters here are printed round s, and the lower-case initial of the second alternative is retained.
The eccentricity is specified as being in dress, customs, and similar matters. This completes the preceding person's description; historical extrauagante and custumes remain unmodernized.
Isǒna supplies the adjectival expression with the same unusual or eccentric sense. The round s and caron are visible, agreeing with the preceding compounds rather than the long-ſ forms elsewhere.
Iſonji means to miss when shooting, here with a bow. The Portuguese ar- continues into arco on the next row; the verb's ita form is retained as printed.
Co completes arco, followed by “and so on,” so the failure-to-hit sense is not restricted absolutely to one weapon. This is a gloss continuation, not another Japanese form.

runs.text: O ir de praya em praya.

lines.note: Iſozzutai denotes going from shore to shore. Its doubled zz is part of the printed romanization and is not simplified or reinterpreted as a Portuguese letter sequence.
Iſuye means to bring someone down or make them fall/sit by a shot. The means are supplied in the next row; the printed aßentar retains its double-s ligature.
The action of Iſuye is performed with an arrow or a shot/projectile. Historical frecha is retained, and pilouro is not replaced by a more specific modern weapon term.

Iſſabaqi means to loosen or disarrange the hair. Only one l is printed before the right rule; removing the bootstrap's extra l preserves the physical division cabel / los, without adding an absent hyphen.
Los completes cabellos. The example says that the hair is loose or disordered; enlargement supports the t of iſsabaite rather than OCR r, while the printed mixed long-ſ/round-s sequence is retained.

runs.text: os cabellos ſoltos. Mas não he palaura boa, nẽ

lines.note: The Portuguese completes the loose-hair description and begins a warning that this is not a good expression. The first word visibly reads es in this impression; the expected Portuguese os is not silently substituted.
The warning continues that the expression is not used in Cami. Meliùs introduces the preferred Japanese wording Camiuo vchimi- / daite iru; Cami is a regional name inside the Portuguese apparatus.

Daite iru completes the recommended expression vchimidaite iru for having disordered hair. This roman continuation remains attached to the alternative begun after Meliùs, rather than forming an independent lemma.
Iſſacu is explained through fitotçu tçucuru, making one thing, and glossed as a work a person makes or completes independently. The Portuguese sentence continues in the next physical row.

runs.text: ſi faz, ou acaba. ¶ Itẽ, permet. Hũ

lines.note: This completes the independently made or finished work. The paragraph then introduces a transferred meaning, with Hũ beginning the explanation “a saying or opinion” below.

The transferred gloss is a saying or opinion, illustrated by iſſacuuo yǔ, to state one. The scan has two long-ſ forms after the initial i, restoring the missing consonant; Di- starts the divided Portuguese infinitive.
Zer completes Dizer: to express one's opinion or saying. The comma immediately after the completed infinitive is printed and is retained despite its unusual placement.
Iſſacujit denotes the day before yesterday. The printed ending jit is retained rather than expanded to a modern romanization of the Japanese compound.
The alternative vototoino yo identifies the night before last. The Portuguese has Antõtẽ with nasal signs over o and e, followed by joined ànoite; enlargement corrects the bootstrap's Antãtẽ ancite.
This Iſſai means one dish, paraphrased as fitotçuno ſai. Its first capital I is a narrow, lightly printed sort beside two long-ſ forms; the nasal abbreviation in Hũa is preserved.

runs.text: De nenhũa maneira quando ſe junta com

lines.note: A separate homonymous Iſſai means “in no way” when combined with a negative. The scan shows both long-ſ forms, whereas the bootstrap omitted one; the following row completes the condition.
This completes the restriction to negative constructions. It distinguishes the negative adverbial use from the “one dish” entry above and the “all” construction below.

Iſſaino supplies the “all” expression. The surviving small initial is read as lowercase i, not the bootstrap's extra la; it is weakly printed. The far-right Iſſaiqiǒ. is a separate catchword and is recorded in its own zone.
